utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have to sit down straight away because we don't have much time. Mr. Registrar. Would you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to welcome all the people in the courtroom and our witness who stayed over during the weekend. I'd like to say good afternoon to the Prosecutor, the ladies and gentlemen of the Defence counsel, the accused, and everybody else present in the courtroom here today. Without further ado, I'm going to give the floor to the registrar. I think he has an IC number to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The list of 1D documents tendered through Witness A shall be given Exhibit number IC 424. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to continue the cross-examination of this witness. According to the calculations, the Defence has 107 minutes left. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. I'd like to continue the topic of the old bridge that we were discussing. And you testified and said that on the 8th of November the tank was targeted -- the bridge was targeted with a tank; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You said that there were about 60 shells fired?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps more; no less though.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And there were four targetings, one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the combat fits of the tank.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down, please. It is impossible to translate at this rate. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that during -- yes. I've been asked by the Judges to slow down so as not to overlap, so let me finish my question before you begin your answer. Do you know that from the positions of the BH army, while the tank was shooting at the old bridge anybody shot at the tank?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second day, yes, but not on the first day. The commander of the 1st Battalion, Esad Kostic, who is still alive, shot on the 10th of November in the morning at the tank from Kamenica bridge targeting the tank from the left bank, but he missed by the height of the cupola. But the man is alive and he lives 50 metres from Kamenica bridge today and you can check that out with him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not my name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Captain, once again let's go back -- or, rather, I'd like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down. It is impossible to translate two people talking at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 2.000 -- from Cekrk to the old bridge, I've been walking around there for 25 years. I know the exact distance to the half metre, and I can tell you exactly. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Captain, my question was this. It was very specific.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead General sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the 8th of November --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the 8th of November did anyone from BH army positions fire at the tank?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No they did not I would have fired but I did not have any grenades, any shells. I guarantee with my head that nobody used any shells and nobody shot, as far as I know, because all I saw was the barrel of the tank from behind the house. I couldn't see anything else. Had I put my head out I would have been shot.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, Witness, I asked you for brief answers. I just asked you one thing.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see a single shell but if I had 20 shells I would have attacked the tank and shot at it, but I didn't. I didn't have a single one. I was on the right bank of the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, sir. Your Honour, if the witness could be instructed to just wait and not interrupt. Allow Mr. Praljak to ask the question, then pause, and then answer so that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We want to get all of your answers, but we do need -- and we're killing the translators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is also true as far as Mr. Praljak is concerned. Please wait for the answer given by the witness before going ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge, some of you are asking me to speed up, like Mr. Praljak; others are asking me to slow down. So what am I going to do? Am I going to slow down or speed up? Or shall I take it at my rate and tell you what I saw in my own words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, try and strike a balance between fast and slow, a middle ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know whether anybody, any commanders of your battalion or your brigade or the command of the 4th Corps, did anybody tell UNPROFOR, report to UNPROFOR that a tank was targeting the old bridge?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that the operation to liberate the eastern part of Mostar began on the morning of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I personally took part in that action.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that I was in charge of that operation; I was in command?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, General, sir. I met Jasmin Jaganjac and your other generals who were on the left bank and who left me, abandoned me in Podvelezje.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that I issued an order to protect the old bridge on the night between the 15th and 16th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir. And I personally provided security with planks and tyres. It wasn't the HVO; it was my battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that that was supposed to be done with 40 men, not with tyres at the time but with planks and steel construction?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You spoke about an English soldier who on the 9th of November filmed the falling of the old bridge.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't an English soldier. He was a Scotsman or Irish. But I can guarantee that he was either a Scotsman or Irishman.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know what time on the 9th of November he placed his camera to film the falling of the old bridge?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that after that, afterwards, he was transferred to Sarajevo with an escort, security provided by the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir, and he disappeared that night.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that he immediately boarded an UNPROFOR aircraft and left Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the cassette, the tape that he taped the toppling of the old bridge he did not hand over to television Sarajevo but he took it outside the country?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So that rounds off the topic of the old bridge, and we'll move on to another area. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And for that, may I have the usher's assistance, please, and take this map to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Captain, you said that you had four platoons in your company, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And you said that you had four commands. On this map can you indicate the positions of the commands of the 1st, 2nd and 3rd and 4th platoon?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry I don't have my glasses with me. The 1st Platoon was at Cekrk. The 2nd platoon was at Gojka Vukovic's house in the Gojka Vukovic local commune.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you leave the map and indicate that to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st Platoon was at Cekrk. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you mark the spot and put a number 1 there, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And mark the second position with a number 2. The 3rd platoon with a number 3.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. That's at Semovac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And number 4 for the fourth position.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ruza hotel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me where your company's headquarters and command was.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Ruza hotel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then put a number 5 there.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here you are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you tell me where the command of your battalion was located?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have Bojnas, we had battalions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well, then. Where was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the Partizan cinema hall at Santic -- Aleksa Santic Street number 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, show us the position of the Kamenica bridge.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And put a number 6 there. You said there was another bridge which was built, the Bunur bridge.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, General, sir. There were four bridges. Four bridges existed, two in Santiceva street, one in Cernica, and two in Donja Mahala. The small bridge, Tito's bridge, and another bridge by Gojka Vukovica house, so you got that mixed up, General. Which one do you want me to draw in now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In Bunur.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in Cernica. I can't see it. It's not on this map. It's not there. In Cernica, between Fejceva [phoen] and Cernica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'll provide you with another map, then, and you can draw it in that one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you get my glass for me please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where are your glasses, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They're in that other room over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go and fetch them then. Go on. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you place your initials on the first map, please, Witness, your initials on that first map and then I'd like an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, an IC number for map number one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number IC 425.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the registrar, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Now my microphone doesn't seem to be working. Something's happened to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark the four bridges on the other map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, it seems that the witness cannot hear Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On this map indicate the four bridges across the Neretva River that were built after the bridges were destroyed in 1992, between the left and right banks.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first was the Kamenica bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then put a number 1 there, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Here it is. It was born there. I bathed in the river there. The second bridge was over here, and the third bridge was between the Lucki bridge and Glozdane [phoen], over here at Riznice. The fourth was between the hotel, the Bristol Hotel, and Tito's villa. It was built by the army and we repaired it. They are four small bridges.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Put a number 4 there then, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is, number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you just tell us where the headquarters of your battalion was?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Santiceva street, number 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark that, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, by the Partizan cinema.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You said that at least those two bridges were opened in March 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And you also said that Kamenica was destroyed on the 10th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Damaged, not destroyed. Your tank started targeting it again, but you failed to hit it and then you used Maljutkas.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And what about the Bunur bridge?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bunur bridge was destroyed, sir, when you brought in a convoy of food, General, sir, when you started distributing the food you destroyed the bridge. Your Honour, Judge, between the 25th and 26th of August, 1993, at 2.00 a.m., Sanica Malavicnika [phoen], he's still alive, woke me up at 3.00 and said, "The bridges are gone." And that was when I was really -- that was the first time in my life I was afraid of the river Neretva. So, General, sir, that's the truth of it, just as I am sitting here. You can check that out. If it's not true, I won't leave here until we finish the whole war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Check. I won't be going anywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Calm down, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me and I answered. If my answer is not true, I'm here to be held liable before the Court. I'm a principled man.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can we now place P 047285. Would you sign this map so we can get an IC number for it.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this white margin? This is where your tank was destroyed, the one who fired on the first day, that 9th of May. It was hit by the red arrow from Podvelezje. You asked me when it was first destroyed. All the shells were collected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the casings, Your Honour, you can get them when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC 426, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This destroyed tank is to be seen on this photograph. Behind this tower that killed five of my men after the fall of Kamenica. This tower was made by Austria 120 years ago. It was the best fortification for many miles around. You saw everything, just didn't see Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must warn the witness, Your Honours. Obviously previous instructions were not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please try to answer exclusively the questions of Mr. Praljak. If the Judges find that additional questions should be asked of you, we will ask them. You are not here to continue the war, so please keep calm and answer Mr. Praljak's questions. Mr. Praljak, proceed. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] So P 04785. The Prosecution attached this document to this witness's statement. Could we move into private session for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: 3D 00779, please, now, and then we can conclude. 3D 00779. Document dated 8th October, 1993, that I signed, and in this order we read: "Flights of aircraft are hereby forbidden unless authorised by the commander of the Main Staff and unless they are used for medevacuations." Is that written there?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the rest of the answer. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any flights after this date?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When did you notice any flights?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I was in Hum when a tyre fell and destroyed half of the Mahala. There was a BBC reporter there. It fell in December. Don't ask me for an exact date. I'm not a 9-year-old child who would exaggerate such a thing and make a mountain out of a molehill. I'm not a child who claims that he had his bones broken when he was written by a wasp. I don't know when it fell but I -- I forgot the date. They kept falling until new year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain, you seem to be in a verbal delirium. General Praljak is showing you a document of the 8th October, 1993, whereby he bans flights, and he's asking you: After that date, to the best of your knowledge, were there any flights by aircraft? You are telling us that there was a tyre that caused damage and destruction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But after that date, did you see an agricultural plane flying over Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these operations always took place after 10.00 p.m. Since Donja Mahala and Cekrk were known for strong winds, you can't hear a thing. You -- the strongest winds blow through Cekrk. You don't see these things until they fall and destroy everything around. All the detonations were between 11.00 p.m. and 3.00 a.m. I didn't see or hear a thing because of the strong winds that were blowing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that there were winds. What we want to know is whether there were planes. Did you hear or see a plane after the 8th of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour, neither heard nor seen because everything took place in the dark. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'll move on to another topic now. 3D 00736, please. That is a document that is already in evidence. It will soon be on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but it's not there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: 3D 00736 is the number. 3D 00736. Here it is. Do you know Mr. Arif Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's his order for attack issued on the 15th September, 1993, and because this material is very complex I'll only ask you if you are aware that an order for attack was issued at HVO lines on that day and whether you know that several days after that a massive operation began against the territories then controlled by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At the end of this document -- can we see the last page, please? It's a brigade order. It's -- it's an order by Semir Drljevic. Do you know Mr. Semir Drljevic?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: His nickname was Lovac, "the hunter." He's one of the real commanders.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you look at the last page, the Croatian side? Do you see the ABH stamp and the signature of Mr. Drljevic?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, 3D 00740, please. 3D 00740. It's a combat order of the command of the 4th Corps of the same date, 15th September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you turn to the last page. Do you recognise the signature of Mr. Arif Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, I would kindly ask that the captain be shown this map that was developed based on these two documents. Can I have the usher's assistance, please. Captain, this map was drawn based on these two documents. It's a very precise map, and it depicts the attack of the BH army as it was supposed to be from the north to the south. And since you were familiar with the operation, could you please look at the map and tell me whether you know that the map -- the plan of attack was indeed this, that this attack was supposed to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about the attack, but I have not seen the map. I can only tell you where my area of responsibility in the attack was. I can explain it to you, if you want to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The south zone, the last one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark it with number 1.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, did you capture Hum hill at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not, because I went to Visnjica. My mission was to capture Austrian bunkers from which you fired at Donja Mahala with a silencer. I can draw it for you. I should, because we didn't know about those emplacements, about those nests.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark with an arrow and number 2 the direction you took.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you sign the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May we have an IC number for the map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given Exhibit number IC 427, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, does the name Esad Sejtanic seem familiar?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And do you know, Witness, that he wrote a book called "Hercegovci: At the Doors of -- at the Flaming Doors of Bosnia"?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I haven't read it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: May we have the next exhibit, 3D 00749 placed on e-court, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the map I'm not sure whether the number 2 the witness was adopting one of the arrows already marked on the map. He was asked to mark an arrow. I must admit my eyes don't pick up an arrow. I wonder if for future reference the witness could be invited to mark more clearly, more specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, General Praljak mentioned the map and the operation that you waged. We see a green arrow which curves towards the right. Now, you explained to us that you attacked the Austrian bunkers where there were people who were shooting there with rifles and silencers. Now, does the arrow correspond to the route you took or is there another direction that you took towards the Austrian bunker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does correspond to that, Your Honour. We went from Donja Mahala up towards the hill. It wasn't a straight line. It's says an elevation at an angle of 60 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Continue, Mr. Praljak. A number for the map, please. [In English] Continue, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] 3D 00749 is the next number. It is a book which has been translated. And I didn't supply a translation last time, so we're coming back to that now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Captain, on page 180 of that book, it's the very next page --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have a number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Page 180. The next page. The page after this one. So turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 779, did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No. 00749, 3D 00749. May we turn to the next page, please. May we have the next page displayed, the top of it. It is page 180.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it, 180 and 81.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Take a look at the second paragraph on page 180, and we'll go through this text very quickly. "The established defence lines facing the Serb forces were not active in combat terms. However, there was a lot of black marketeering going on along those same lines, and most of all black marketeering in the sources that were lacking." Do you know about this black marketeering?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't in thieves or black marketeering or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on page 181 it says: "According to what the fighters knew, that Sefer Halilovic with forces from Bosnia was in -- was located in Jablanica. There was spontaneous singing, and the song is Bosnia is being cleansed of the Ustashas under the leadership of so-and-so. Do you know that song?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, come on. What are you asking me about? I don't know any of this. This is the first time that I have read this. We are the children of Partizans, so don't ask me about songs like this. When I say I never saw anything like this then believe me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Captain, in the next paragraph it says: "Within the frameworks for preparations for planned operations, it -- the possibility was openly raised of the Serb side helping us in a direct artillery support and in providing us with the critical resources and materiel, and first and foremost, selling a large number of artillery projectiles of different calibres." And then in continuation it goes on to say: "I attended one of the meetings up at the line facing the Serb forces in the village of Busek, where Safet Orucevic, Fatima Leho, and Sefkija Dziho defined the conditions under which the Serb side would assist our combat operations." And so on and so forth. It says the Serb side agreed to provide a howitzer with a -- fully manned with a crew. And then it goes on to say on the next page that as for cooperation so far, Safet Orucevic told the commander of the Nevesinje Brigade, Novica Pusic -- or, rather, he made him a present of an almost new Golf car. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, General, sir, but this is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there, so I can't really say anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, the next paragraph: "We all expected a great deal from the agreement that had been reached, and perhaps this led us to be more forward in planning our future combat operations, which objectively speaking, given our force and strength and conditions in the area could not give any significant results. But be things as it may, my unit," that is to say Mr. Sejtanic's unit, "in cooperation with the 48th Mountain Brigade was given the assignment of attacking key facilities in the HVO defence, that is to say Hum hill." And underneath that it says: "In the period between the 10th and 18th of September, intensive reconnaissance work was carried out of the area of attack and features of attack," and it goes on to say towards the end of page 182: "Once again in the course of the 19th of September we analysed the tasks assigned us and looked into the preparations that had been organised and became informed of combat operations which were being implemented by the BH army along the axis of Dreznica, Vrdi, and Goranci." Do you know that that was so?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And towards the end of that page it says: "During the night without any problems at all, units were brought into the town of Mostar from where in the early hours of the morning they were supposed to move ahead to the features to be attacked. The units -- the unit that was to attack Hum hill was led by my deputy, Tahir Turajlic." This document -- well, let me ask you one more thing. The units within the urban town had initial success along the Balinovac settlement axis and had a lot of Serbian artillery support. Now, do you know about this artillery support on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, General, I don't know about this, anything about this at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And may we now turn to page 184, please. Or, never mind. I think I've exhausted the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me carry on from what General Praljak was asking you. He was reading excerpts from a document, a book written by a BH army -- former BH army soldier, and he referred to page 180, 81, and so on, and these pages seem to establish that there was an agreement between the BH army and the Serb side and that this agreement seemed to materialise on the day when you attacked Hum hill. Now, this is what we can read in paragraph 3, more specifically on page 183, where it says that there was Serb artillery support. Now, to the best your knowledge, did the Serbs in actual fact aid and assist you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a company commander. I wasn't -- I was only the in Donja Mahala, so I really can't say. I don't know. I can't say yes, and I can't say no. But I was just the commander of a small unit company at Cekrk. I can't tell you. I can't say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But to the best of your recollections, when you attacked the hill, everybody knows in military terms that when one attacks you must have artillery support. Now, when you attacked, did the artillery come into play, or did you just storm the Austrian bunkers without any artillery support?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Alone, sir. We didn't have a single shell, a single grenade. My group at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, continue. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Captain, you know that platoons don't have any artillery.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any artillery support. You have your witnesses. You can ask them. All we had was hand grenades.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On page 183, let us just note: "The results of the combat operations against -- of the 4th Corps units were terrible. While they were pulling out to their initial positions we had more than 30 dead and about 100 wounded, heavily wounded or less seriously wounded, and combat morale reached its lowest ebb."

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This isn't -- none of this is true and correct. This man is mad.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I intervene? In the answer, the complete answer of the witness wasn't recorded, and I wrote this down. He said: "We went as sabotage men and just had hand bombs." The Diverzanti or "sabotage group" was left out on lines 20 and 21. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement you said that that Donja Mahala was destroyed by the Serbs 90 per cent and the HVO destroyed it 10 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that in Mostar in 1992 -- the Urbicid of Mostar, 1992. This was the title of a book that was published.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was compiled jointed about by the Croatian -- by Croatian and Bosnian intellectuals, town planners, architects, photographers, and so on. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, do you know, and may we have a page from the book displayed on the overhead projector, please. Take a look at Donja Mahala which has been photocopied from the book. The red legend in the book says that it is the area of total destruction. Do you agree that the red area was a zone of total destruction?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: 1992, Captain.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. That's not correct. They were destroyed but not as much as this. I don't know -- this isn't true for Donja Mahala. It's true for Mostar but not for Donja Mahala. I don't know who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: May we take a look at some photographs. 3D 00784, for example. 3D 00784. Can we zoom in on that, please. Is this a small street in Donja Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my alleyway, Cevin [phoen] Alley, and I know every house there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Next document 3D 00784. 3D 00784, please. 3D 00784 is the number. Ah, no. It seems to be 88. 0988, please. The next picture. 0988. The next photograph. Do you recognise this in Donja Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir. It is the mosque by my house.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And now the next number, 0990. 0990.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We're looking at the same photograph. We need the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Cekrk. It's right at the edge of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was it completely destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is -- compared to what it was like in 1993, well, no, it's been repaired since then. I slept here, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain, General Praljak has shown you three photographs, and it seems -- he seems to want to show that what we can see of Donja Mahala, and you yourself recognise the mosque and the ruins of the building, on the basis of what Mr. Praljak is putting forward, this apparently had been destroyed by the Serbs. Do you agree with that or not, or was it destroyed by HVO shelling? What was your point of view on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was destroyed by the Serbs. However, these are buildings on the outskirts. This is my primary school. All the people were in there and refugees, too, and all this was blown up with two shells. You can't see the photographs of the area between Donja Mahala and the main road where one explosion destroys five houses. These are large buildings, the 7th elementary school at Cekrk and so on. One shell can destroy it on. Now, had you seen what it looked like after the 19th, well, Hiroshima cannot be compared. It looks better now. They dropped everything on it except an atom bomb. We were spared an atom bomb. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The witness has testified to these photographs, and we have a book which was published as a joint effort.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, had a -- the building been destroyed like this, there wouldn't have been 1.000 refugees sleeping there. I'm not a child. Don't show me things like this. I'll stay two months if need be. And in this elementary school in 1993 there were 1.000 people accommodated there. There was a kitchen. There was a first aid part and so on. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: This is a book called "Urbicid." It was jointly made by Croats and Muslims in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not interested at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I just want to review one more document. Regarding the number residents by local commune made in March. Document 3D 00780. In March 1993, on the 11th of March, there was a census in Mostar, and there is a breakdown by local commune. It's a two-page document. Can we look at table number 2, Captain. Second column.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Donja Mahala.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. There were 2.042 people, seven one hundred twelve [as interpreted] households, 101 men -- sorry, 1.001 men, 1.041 women, 517 refugees, local residents 1.024, 500-something Croats, and 682 Muslims. Do you agree with these numbers?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. You did not list everything. You didn't list much, in fact. This is not true, General. Somebody wrote it to suit their ends. I, as company commander, say publicly that this is a lie. This is maybe a preparation for something else. Why isn't this document signed? I would have -- I would bite his head off now. Why isn't it signed? I can guarantee, I can vouch that this is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to repeat that this Witness needs to be cautioned. He's beginning to threaten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just threatened to kill the person who made this document. You say you contest their figures. We note that, but there is no need to issue threats to people who are not present in the first place. We note your protest. And, Mr. Praljak, I'll just ask the registrar to tell me how much time you've used up already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we understand your feelings sometimes when you are getting more and more excited. You have been there fighting in Mostar, and of course General Praljak was there in his other capacity. I understand this, but at the same time, as it was already many times mentioned to you, you have to be concentrating on the questions which are asked by General Praljak and then to answer them. And you do not -- you are not here to fight your private war between yourselves. It is another question if that in that situation I am a Judge for the rights of the accused, and I am for the rights of General Praljak to ask questions. It is again another question if it is the best of the worlds if -- as a matter of fact if two former combatants who fought against each other are asking about each other's position. I tell you as a private person. At the same time, again, I would like to underline and emphasise that I am for the rights of the accused to ask questions. It is what I would have liked to say, and I hope that the situation will calm down and we can finish with this examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really have to apologise. I've just seen that this was made by the social institute for -- by the institute for social welfare. It was on the left bank of the Neretva, in fact. I didn't see that before. I saw it -- thought it was the local communes who made this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have used 90 minutes. That is one hour and a half. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'll be concluding.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You just said that it was the institute for social welfare that prepared this document. It bears a date. It bears a number. It's an official document, in other words, so it must have been signed and somebody prepared it officially, and the date is the 11th of March, 1993. That is before the conflict in Mostar. Is that visible there?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And it says that Croats in Donja Mahala numbered 266. Is that written there?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know where those Croats left after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them left before the conflict, before the 9th of May, of their own will to the other side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Which side?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The west side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thanks. Tell me one more thing. I'll show you two photographs, and you will show me on them where HVO dug trenches at Stupan. You look at the photographs and tell me where the HVO drug trenches at Stotina [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer, I have to tell you that the Spanish Battalion of the UNPROFOR levelled it all with bulldozers. I watched it with my own eyes from the Hum hill. And this photograph is not good. It was -- the trenches were dug closer to the woods, the weekend cottages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General -- in fact, Captain, you said -- you said the Spanish Battalion levelled it all. When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the Dayton Accords, sometime in 1995, 1996. You seal the heaps here. You see the heaps here, and you see that it's all levelled.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak cannot be heard had. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you put a line where the HVO trenches were, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Put a number 1.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And now draw an arrow in the direction where you had your reconnaissance positions. On the same photograph.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Close to this edge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Put a number 2 and sign it.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me to the interpreter. That will be given Exhibit number IC 428. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On this front side here where this man is standing, were there any bunkers or sandbags?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were connecting trenches lined with stone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where it is written "HDZ."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Raise it so we can see it all.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the top of Stotina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So take it easy and tells us where it was.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the place from which the tank fired at Kamenica. You placed a tank there, and we fired at it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And where were the trenches?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But not where you drew them there?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were connecting trenches lined with stones and sandbags. The trenches were closer to the weekend cottages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sign it, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number, please, for the first and second photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given Exhibit number IC 248, Your Honours -- sorry, 429, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When you attacked, how many soldiers defended Stotina, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not able to count them. I was attacking Visnjica. I wasn't attacking Stotina. I think I told you that before. I was attacking a hundred metres to the other side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But you did reconnaissance prior to that. In your estimate, how many soldiers defended Stotina?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but there were 40 or 50 per shift.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My last question: You said that Mr. Resulovic [phoen] was hit, was shot at the Neretva when he was carrying Manjerka.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to the mosque I said, where the air bomb fell.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: This army dish, was it purely quartermaster's equipment?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was just carrying food. It was a small army dish for food. He just -- he was shot at the entrance to Orucevica Sokak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether this dish was part of military equipment or civilian equipment?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can use it for both. It was a white dish. It wasn't the green olive-grey army colour. You hit also Zulfo Maric in the same way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it with my own eyes. Don't you try to sell me this. He was washing his dish in the Neretva. And you also killed a woman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to give the floor to another counsel. The fourth Defence counsel, and then we go to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll group my questions according to topics, and please try to answer them as best as possible for the benefit of all of us and the Trial Chamber included. If you remember the map on which last Thursday you drew the demarcation line between the HVO and ABiH, it went along Santic Street and the Bulevar, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on which day. Lines moved, shifted four to five times in the course of combat operations, and it wasn't the same in May, July, or September. They shifted a lot both ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm only interested in the line before the 9th of May and on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then there were no lines at that time at all. As far as I know, there were no separation lines then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, up to the 9th of May, on what positions were your units located? Did you hold Donja Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We held Podvelezje, facing the Serbian side. I was commander of the sector for the defence line at Podvelezje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witnesses told us before that the separation line was exactly as you showed it. One of the witnesses said, I quote, "It was always that way." And the ABiH, before it clashed with the HVO, held a part of that line, and the HVO held --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. The army held the 3rd school, Hotel Mostar, and Vranica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It has to slow down. The interpreter didn't catch this question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will ask my question again because the interpreters did not manage. My question was: Was Donja Mahala, prior to the 9th of May, 1993, under the control of the BH army or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The area of Cernica, until the 9th of May, 1993, was it under the control of the BH army or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cernica was held by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina until the 9th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the area between Santiceva Street and the Neretva River? Until the 9th of May was it held by the BH army or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To us it was a free area. There were no troops. It was an area where Hotel Bristol was and the kitchen. The army was in Hotel Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From your answer I see that an all these areas I mentioned were held by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina prior to the 9th of May, Cernica and others.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let us clear up some details about the 9th of May. In the statement you made and we received, in paragraph 9 you said that approximately 1.200 people came on the 9th of May to Donja Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were expelled to the left bank; right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But in your statement you said they were either expelled or they fled. If necessary, I can remind you of the precise contents of your statement, but I quoted from it. Out of those 1.200, to the best of your knowledge, how many were expelled and how many had fled?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know that. The lists were made by the Donja Mahala local commune. I don't know who was expelled and who fled. It's not in my power to say so. I saw the lists that they made, so I cannot confirm either way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On those lists was a distinction made between those who were expelled and those who came of their own will, who fled?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So there was only one list?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know, because I didn't make the lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But there was one list, one list?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one list for everybody, the elderly, women, children, men. As the families came in they were listed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So in that single list it was not possible to distinguish between those who were expelled and those who had fled?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Croats who are listed here as residents of Donja Mahala in March 1993, and you say that prior to the 9th of May, 1993, most of them had left of their own will to the west bank.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But others stayed with us and spent the whole war with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a case where a Muslim, before the conflict of the 9th of May, crossed from one part of Mostar to the other?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on this side. Mostly from mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, do you know that the following day after the conflict, that is to say already on the 10th of May, Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban signed an agreement on a cease-fire, a cessation to all conflicts. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately I don't have time to present the documents to you because some other documents are more important, but you can believe me when I tell you that they did do that. They did reach an agreement on the 10th of May and issued orders to that effect. Now, do you know that on the 12th of May General Sefer Halilovic and Milivoj Petkovic reached an agreement on the cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we present a set of documents to the witness that I prepared. I don't know whether you have it. It's this bundle this yellow bundle. And on e-court, may we have P 02352. It is an agreement between Halilovic and Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I don't mind you showing him the document, but he says he doesn't know about it, so what purpose does it serve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge, it took me three days from the 9th of May to break through from Cekrk. You can't imagine the kind of situation we were in. I could just panelling an area of 100 kilometres. I couldn't see this, I didn't hear this. So I'm a complete layman where things like this are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me to explain. I'm not going to ask anything about the authenticity of the agreement, the way in which it was reached, the conditions of the agreement, or anything else. But I am going to ask him about displaced persons, that topic, because it's a topic that the witness deals with in his statement and he dealt with it in the examination-in-chief. I think it is a very relevant topic, and the document will serve as a basis for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Anyway, we're not going to go into the entire document, but look at Article 5 of the document, please, where the generals of the two armies agree on the following: "Both sides will assist the return of displaced persons to their own property or homes." Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, do you know what the concept "displaced persons" refers to? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't explain that to you now either.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll tell you and then it will be easier for us to discuss the issue. Displaced persons is a concept denoting people who within the same place of residence changed a local commune, from Mostar -- going from East Mostar to West Mostar is considered to be a displaced person. Tell me, do you know of any activities linked to the agreement made by the two armies about the return of displaced persons to their homes?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at document 4D 00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Witness, I'm going to go to the heart of the matter. There was a document that you were shown where the Defence refers to Article 5, which is titled "Return Of Displaced Persons." It is a document dated the 12th of May, 1993. Now, my question is an extremely simple one. In Donja Mahala on the 13th of May, 1993, did Muslims who had been expelled or moved out of Donja Mahala, did they return to West Mostar? It's yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there were war operations. I couldn't know that. There was a war still going on. There was still shooting in Mahala. Nobody could cross the line. That's my conclusion. Whoever approached was either killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll ask the witness the same question, but with your permission could I follow the proceedings that I merit should lead up to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you look at 4D 00496, please. While you're looking for the document and while we get it up on e-court, I'll tell you what it's about. It's a report on talks conducted between Sefer Halilovic and Arif Pasalic and which was recorded by the corresponding service in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Counsel. What is it, this? Are they telephone conversations or what?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They are intercepts of telephone conversations. Perhaps it's not a telephone conversation. The generals will explain to us. They know how this interception was conducted. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] They were ultra-shortwave connections that were intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at this together. We have a statement by Arif Pasalic on the topic we're discussing now, and in this first part we have Arif Pasalic's answer. Pasalic says, "The whole day we've been discussing the exchange of prisoners. I received 57, and I sent them 37." Then I'm going to skip over a sentence, and then you goes on to say, "Today we are continuing the transfer of the population to the other side, to their homes. The lists that we have compiled, because there was a number of controversial issues there, and they are afraid that they could infiltrate some special ones there as special groups, and I explained to them that it is totally unfounded. Today we shall transport over to the other side approximately 1.000 persons to return to their homes. Today I should get Zijo Demirovic to this side. We already have a rough list. Therefore, I would ask if you could wait until I bring Demirovic here as a leading person of the party. The mufti and others are also here. So we shall have a consultation and could send the list during the day or in the evening." The conversation based on this document was held on the 27th of May, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I see this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you see the date there, the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From this conversation it would emerge that the lists of persons who are to cross over to the other side, obviously from the east to the west, should be done in cooperation with the representatives of the BH army, the political parties, the Party of Democratic Action, and the muftis; is that right? Does that emerge from this?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about this, whether it emerges from this, because I'm reading it for the first time, but I suppose this was in agreement with HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, tell us, do you have any knowledge that any lists were compiled of persons wishing to cross from one bank to the other bank of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I say with full responsibility that I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps ever hear that in the Djacki Dom in West Mostar a list of Muslims was being compiled, Muslims who said they voluntarily wished to cross over to the other side, to the east? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I swear to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From this document, if we assume it is a truthful document, would it emerge that in May attempts were being made by people who had left their homes to return to their homes, including the departure of Muslims from the east bank to the west bank? Would that emerge?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say it does emerge from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we agree that in May we cannot speak of any persecutions and expulsions of Muslims from their homes in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should ask them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you. Once the conflicts had ceased, once Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic had reached an agreement on a cease-fire and after the heads of the armies tried to agree on how to resolve the conflicts, and all this was going on in the month of May, do you have any knowledge to the effect that in May the HVO persecuted Muslims, so that in the second half of the month hundreds of Muslims were expelled from their homes or anything similar to that?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, then, when?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was shooting where we were all the time. There was no cease-fire where we were. There was constant shooting, as far as I know, in May. There was no cease-fire. There was shooting all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you said that on the 9th of May about 1.200 people arrived - that's what you've said - and you said that a total of about 2 to 3.000 refugees or displaced persons arrived --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the next period. Not that day, in the period that followed. I apologise. That wasn't that day. I said in the period that followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to quote you now. You said on Thursday in the transcript on page 77 to 78 of the transcript, you said: "Over the next two, three, or four months a number inhabitants rose to 5.000, of which about 3.000 were old residents and 2.000 were displaced persons or refugees. I'm not sure because I wasn't there." That's what you've said.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is how it was recorded in the transcript. To continue: "All I know is that 2.000 people arrived in the space of just one month." Now, Witness, I consider that the departure of even a single individual is a great tragedy, and I'm very sorry to have to count all the people together, so please don't hold that against me when I am talking about a total number. If you say that 1.200 arrived in May, the 9th of May, in fact, and if you also say that nobody returned to their homes from -- to West Mostar, and if at the end of the entire conflict there was a total of 2.000, that means 800 more than those who were there on the 9th of May, what is this all about, and what statements are these? What month was it when most of the people arrived in Donja Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were people who had flats in one -- on the Bulevar and houses in Donja Mahala, in the Avenija. Most people arrived in July after their expulsion from North Camp; in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. That is the answer I expected, because to my -- according to my information, that corresponds to what actually happened. And my next question was supposed to be whether we agree that in fact it was after the beginning of all-out conflict, that is to say after the 30th of June there was a large population displacement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move on to another topic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much longer do you need? How many minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need a lot of time, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not a lot of time. You had 25 minutes, and we'll deduct the number of minutes you've already used from that number, which means that you have five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague Mr. Karnavas has just told me that I can use his time or part of his time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I thought that Mr. Karnavas had given his time to Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no. Mr. Karnavas, if I might be allowed to interpret his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. We said that the Defence had two hours and 30 minutes for the cross-examination. So, Mr. Registrar, would you do the calculations from the start of Defence time. So if you had two and a half hours, that would be it. Your time is over. One hundred and twenty minutes have been used up, up until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's fine. That suits us. That's just the amount of time that we need to finish our questioning. But shall we take a break now? Is this an opportune moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, take a look at the calculations again, because it is my impression that there's been a mistake. But let's take a break and that will give the registrar enough time to check this out. So I'd like you to calculate the time used on Thursday and the time used today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is -- we are resuming, and we -- you have 30 minutes left according to our arithmetics. Mr. Karnavas, I understood a moment ago that you have given your time to Ms. Alaburic. I said last week, Mr. Karnavas, and you made a speech on behalf of the Defence asking for the right to cross-examine. We among the Judges discussed this, and without revealing any secrets, you know that we did not agree completely amongst us, and there is an opinion that there should be no cross-examination of the destruction of the bridge in Mostar. My colleagues do not agree with me. I now discover with amazement that you have no intention of cross-examining and that you have given your time to Mrs. Alaburic. So please explain what happened between Thursday and Friday that made you abandon your request, your previous position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon, Your Honours. It is not that I have abandoned my request. First of all, let me begin by saying this was a 92 ter witness. In practice, his statement was supposed to come in during the proofing session. The gentleman brought in all sorts of other new material which obviously caused me concern, enough concern for me to request that the post -- that the cross-examination be postponed so I could have the time to evaluate the gentleman's direct examination and contact my investigator and look into matters. That's number one. Number two, I was speaking on behalf of all of the Defence, not just myself, with the exception perhaps for General Praljak, who seemed to think that it was wise to go ahead on his own on his cross-examination. So I think -- out of an abundance of caution, I thought it was necessary for me to -- to have sufficient time to be -- prepare and exercise due diligence. Now, having listened to the cross-examination by Mr. Praljak and by Ms. Alaburic, it appears that a lot of the issues that I think would be necessary to cover are being covered. That's number one. Number two, while I may have some cross-examination for the gentleman, it would appear to me that if I have to balance what I need to get from the gentleman versus what perhaps Ms. Alaburic is trying to elicit from the gentleman, and I put this on the scale, given the limited amount of time I think it would be much more beneficial to have Ms. Alaburic get those points across as opposed to what I have to cross-examine on, and the issues that I have to raise can be raised either through other witnesses or at another point. So that's the purpose. There was no deception of any kind. I just think as a professional I have to call it as I see it. As I indicated on Thursday, yes, I can stand up with just about any witness and do a cross-examination. But that doesn't necessarily mean that's always wise, and a good cross-examination sometimes is no cross-examination, or a limited one, which takes time to prepare. So I'm not trying to -- I don't want to waste the Court's time and I think, I hope I have answered your questions, but if you want some more explanations, fire away with some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Alaburic, you have 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to thank Mr. Karnavas, first, for taking care last Thursday that all the Defence teams have appropriate time to prepare for this cross-examination, and I thank him also for giving me his own time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would now like to discuss briefly your knowledge about Bosniaks or Muslims who used to be HVO soldiers. Are you aware that there were Muslim soldiers in the HVO as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly from the corrigenda to your statement, you served also as assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For security.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. You just used another term for security. Tell me, in which way did you communicate with your superiors in the security chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By reporting. We had no communications. We went to them to report by night.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: By night. You mean --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after midnight or 1.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did your superiors give you any instructions? Was your attention drawn to certain issues that they believed to be particularly important?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was too low in the chain of command for that. They did not tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you did not get any instructions from them on how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but on a lower level. Security of the line, securing positions, logistical support and such. On a higher level I was not even -- I did not even have access.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that security organs in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had special plans for the Muslims in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us go to the 30th of June, 1993, a date you mentioned several times in your statement. On that day the BH army attacked and captured Tihomir Misic barracks, Bijelo Polje, Vrapcici, Rastane, and that area north of Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, on those locations or, rather, in those territories that until that time were under the control of the HVO, was the HVO mixed in terms of ethnic composition? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the approximate percentage of Muslims in the HVO in those areas?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Proportion was maybe 70 to 30 or 65 to 35, because I wasn't there. I had to stay in Donja Mahala. In that operation, my sole sign many was to secure the line, to hold the line Bulevar-Donja Mahala, so I'm not aware of these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know anything, whether from before or later, as to the Muslims' important role in capturing these areas?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we look at document 5526.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P 05526. It should be the second in your file. It's a document drafted on the 1st of October, 1993, by the district military court in Mostar. It's an all-points alert listing 423 members of the HVO who on the 30th of June, 1993, switched to the ABH units. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
