utterances.text: You can check on page 32 the last name on this list of 423 HVO members of Muslim ethnicity who crossed over the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Then let's look at the next document, P 08497. It's a criminal report by the department of military crime police. The date is after the Dayton Accords, the 5th December, 1994. There are 490 names listed here, but I can draw your attention to the fact that some of them were members of the BH army throughout. So this part about desertion from the HVO and crossing over to the BH army does not concern them. From these two documents, Mr. Salcin, it follows that 423 Muslims, members of the HVO, left the HVO on that day and crossed over to the BH army. Have you ever heard that Muslims deserted from the HVO? Or that they left the HVO, if you don't like the previous term.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they had given an oath. There can be no desertion in my book if there had been no oath. If you want me to believe this list, then you have to show me a proper document showing that these soldiers had taken an oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us assume --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to assume anything. If there was no oath --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you now about these specific names. We don't have time for that. At this moment we're only interested in one thing. Do you have any knowledge that Muslim members of the HVO at some point crossed over to the BH army? And I am now focusing on the 30th of June, 1993, and the 2nd Brigade of the HVO that controlled these territories taken over later by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a lot of lists, but individuals moved between the HVO and the BH army three times a year, or a month depending on where the wages were higher. It was always better in the HVO. The money was better and the logistics were better. We were poor. I'm telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How come that precisely on the 30th of June, 1993, the BH army suddenly had so much more money that all the Muslims from the 2nd Brigade of the HVO crossed over to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you with full responsibility that nobody got a dinar. I didn't get a single Deutschmark during the war. What money are you talking about? We didn't have bread to eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It was you who mentioned money. I only picked it up from you. So you had no knowledge that these soldiers crossed over to the ABH for money's sake?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard that the BH army took control of the Tihomir Misic barracks and all the other territories I mentioned earlier because Muslims within the HVO had disarmed their Croat fellows?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And because they became in those territories members of the -- of the enemy army?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. It was an elite unit of the BH army that captured these territories. There was not a single man from the HVO. They were too afraid of us. And I'm sorry I wasn't involved myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How can you explain this fact then: All the Muslims -- on the 30th of June, 1993, all Muslims who were in the 2nd Brigade of the HVO left the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't explain. I'm not familiar with these things. I'm hearing them for the first time from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move then to another subject, and that's probably the only subject I have enough time left for. In your statement you told us, in paragraph 8, that your company was used only for defence purposes.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. On Thursday and earlier today you told us that you personally led the attack of your group at Visica [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you then explain how come your company was used solely for defence purposes if you with your units went and conquered some areas that had been under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When your mothers and your sisters were being killed by snipers all the time, what would you do when you see your own mother and you were sister-in-law with two small children being shot by snipers? You wouldn't be asking me these things. We started attacking, Your Honours, because they started attacking our women and children. Can you imagine -- can you imagine all our families being held for months in basements where it's 50 degrees centigrade? My mother went blind in a basement, and they had no water all summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They let you question me because you're a woman. You think you can take liberties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you to calm down.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm telling you why we attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, ask your question. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately at what time did you decide that the Donja Mahala inhabitants would be defended --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters are kindly asking speakers to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: We cannot continue like this. Please slow down. Both of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speak calmly, please. Even if you find the questions upsetting, you have to -- you have to calm down, because the Accused have the right to question you. The questions have to be asked, and you must answer calmly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Ms. Alaburic. But before that, I want to ask you something, and I'm sure you can answer calmly. You just said that on the 17th of September you decided to attack because the 200 children were in the basements. It was 40 degrees and more, and we can imagine that situation. When you said that, I wondered immediately about this 17th September attack. Did you decide to attack or was it the commander of the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the commander of my battalion. I didn't know that he received orders. But Semir Drljevic, after the Napalm bombs that were used, all in the space of one night, Your Honour. I'm very sorry, but had you experienced the kind of shelling I lived through, and I already told you God forbid that you should ever experience what we experienced, and I'm one of the few who survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, but you experienced shelling, and for you to -- what you're saying will be understood and heard by many people, so you're going to make an important contribution. You said that you were following orders issued by your commander. So the decision wasn't yours. You were asked to attack; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you remind us, what date did you say was the day when the bombs were thrown and the tyres on Donja Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th of August, the 17th of September, and the last fell sometime in December just before the new year. I know all about that, Ms. Alaburic. I know what it's like.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, take a look at document 4D 00497 now, please. Perhaps we'll find some answers as concerns your military operations on the 17th of September. This is document is a reaction by Sefer Halilovic to an interview by Rasim Delic, which was published in the Zagreb magazine Globus, and this reaction, Sefer Halilovic, on the 1st of May, 1995, sent -- was sent to the President, Alija Izetbegovic, and to the members of the Presidency of the Bosnia-Herzegovina. There are a lot of interesting conclusions but unfortunately we don't have time to go through them all so would you please focus on two of them. The first is point 9, which is upon page 6. And in point 9, after a description of the preparations for a military operation, Sefer Halilovic says the following: "On the 12th of September, the beginning of the operation --" it's point 9. Point 9. "On the 12th of September, the operation began ..." And then a little further on it says: "On the 13th of September, after taking all measures, all the units went to carry out their tasks ..." And then mention is made that the Prozor Battalion entered Uzdol and that crimes were submitted there against the Croatian population which Sefer Halilovic calls "impermissible acts," unlawful acts. Look at item 10 now, please. I think that will be an important item for our conclusions. It relates to operation Neretva, and the overall results of the operation are impressive. Pursuant to an UNPROFOR report, the BH army advanced and liberated more than 450 square kilometres. Tell us, please, Mr. Salcin. Did you have any knowledge whatsoever to the effect that your military activities in mid-September 1993, were part of a broader operation called the Neretva Operation?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, madam, never. Not at all. If you believe -- may Sefer Halilovic and Rasim Delic I saw for the first time on television. I never saw them face-to-face during the war. That's how much they cared for me on the right bank of the Neretva, and I will tell them if I ever meet them. They left all the population down there. They didn't help them at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well you don't need to see the main commander to --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about this. This is the first time I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. I believe you when you say that this is the first time that you have seen the document, but is it the first time that you heard about operation Neretva and these military activities?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is Neretva and there is Neretvica, but I say with full responsibilities that I never heard of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You've just tried to explain to us. Before that I'd like to note that the answer the witness gave was not fully reported. The witness said perhaps this is Neretvica?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the river that flows through Butrovic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: He said that Neretva, the river Neretva exists and Neretvica exists.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And there were operations of Neretva and Neretvica is that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, explain to us what was the Neretvica operation and what was the Neretva operation then?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neretva, it was the fertilised part over there, but as to the other, I don't know. I have no idea about any of this. I haven't lied so far and I'm not going to lie now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So if I understand what you're saying, you're saying you didn't know anything about the Neretva operation but you did know about a Neretvica operation?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about the Neretva operation, but -- I did know about the Neretva operation but not the Neretvica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you knew about Neretva?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What did you know about operation Neretva?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the operation would take place, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let us take a look at page 3 of Sefer Halilovic's document. Halilovic speaks about a team preparing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the interpreters have asked you not to speak at the same time as counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic, on page 3, and it is the beginning of the second section, mentions the leaders of the team. You see that Sefer Halilovic, Suljevic, Bilajac, Karic, Najetovic, Hasan Spahic, Dzankovic, and it says: "The aforementioned team will elaborate necessary documents for the operation named Neretva 93," and the entire document refers to this operation named Neretva 93 in which, as it says, 450 square kilometres of territory was liberated which up until then had been under HVO control. So you knew about that operation?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew about this particular operation. But these are all people from Bosnia. There is not a single man here from Herzegovina. Take a look at the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Salcin. Let's move on to the next document, because my time is running out slowly. The next document is 4D 00498, and I'd like to ask you as a member of the BH army to tell us whether you know something or not. Now, this document is a list of conclusions and assignments for the consultations held among the heads of staff and corps commanders of the BH army held in Zenica on the 21st and 22nd of August, 1993, and the document was signed by Mr. Rasim Delic, commander of the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Take a look at page 6, the signature and stamp there of the Supreme Command. Have you managed to take a look at that? It's on page 6 in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, let's take a look at the contents of that document. Almost all the points are as important, but we're going to focus on what I consider to be the most important and that is item 3. Take a look at item 3 on page 2. Item 3 says as follows: "The war from the territory will continue, and if there is peace on the basis pursuant to the Geneva agreements." Now, Mr. Salcin, let's try and understand this. Does that mean that the BH army had decided to continue the war to take over territory even if Alija Izetbegovic happens to sign a peace agreement?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know that? This is Zenica. I was in the south. I didn't have a civilian telephone. Madam, I didn't have any communication with the old bridge let alone further on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salcin --

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I don't know. I have absolutely no idea. I couldn't contact the old bridge and now you're troubling me with this document that I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salcin, all I'm interested in is to hear whether you have any knowledge to the effect that the BH army had plans to take control over certain territories.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. And I say that with absolute certainty. I in Mostar knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at point 5, the last sentence of point 5. Forms of the arms struggle are being debated, and it is said that more than up to present sabotage operations in the front, intelligence and sabotage operations aimed at the aggressor's front line, behind the front line, and deep in his rear should be used more frequently than before. Now today, on page 23 of today's transcript, you said as a sabotage unit you had hand grenades. Now, were you following instructions on the basis of this document, you and your sabotage group? Did you or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the things that every army does. Yes, we did, and every army does that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next point, which is point 8, that I'd like to look at. In the point 8 we have references to logistics for the army, and I'm going to read sentence 3: "In distributing weapons, ammunition, and military materiel, regardless of the complexity -- complicated delivery across the aggressor's territory, this may be effected through the involvement of all available factors and methods, from friends to enemies, from patriots to war profiteers and traitors from the aggressor's armed units." Do you have any knowledge as to how your units -- your unit came by weapons and ammunition and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We bought it from black marketeers. That is going on today. There's weapons trafficking today.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at point 11 which says as follows: "The state organs of the army, of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, during the armed conflict were -- the organs of state authority of the BH army have throughout the period of armed combat been out of touch with the general directions of the armed forces. State authorities have only partially switched to wartime function, which has resulted in adequate logistical support of the armed forces. "In certain areas state authorities were acting in a destructive way detrimental to the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina by siding with separatist forces, especially the HVO." Now, tell us, Mr. Salcin, do you have any knowledge about what the position held by the BH army was and the leadership of the BH army with respect to the politics and policies of Alija Izetbegovic -- take part in peace negotiations and to arrive at a peaceful solution through negotiations for the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, dear, I am not a politician. I have nothing to do nor do I know anything about political machinations. They didn't reach me, things like that. All I was bent on doing was save my own life and lives. I have nothing -- I know nothing about any of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard that a commander of the BH army who decided on the deployment of military units said that they would continue to fight the war regardless of the policies waged by Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was never in physical contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you ever hear that in the BH army the following policy was promoted: To strengthen one's own units to the maximum. "We'll never be able to wage war against the Serbs because they're too strong, but when we become strong enough then we can start the struggle against the HVO." Did you ever hear anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let us look at point 3 in chapter 2, "Tasks," paragraph 3, point 3, it says: "In all corps offensive actions -- in all corps offensive actions shall be applied to a greater extent than before. Sabotage and intelligence operations must be used on a mass scale, with emphasis on actions just behind the aggressor's front lines and deep in his rear." Now, you told us about these sabotage operations of your own unit. Now, do you know that in a broader area under HVO control there was a series of sabotage operations launched by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My time is up, and because of that I'll have to end there, and I'll have to say that I have completed the cross-examination of this witness, and I thank you, Mr. Salcin, for answering my questions. I hope that you have not been too upset by them.

utterances.speaker: MIRO SALCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any re-examination by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then, Witness, on behalf of my colleagues I'd like to thank you for coming. At times your testimony gave rise to a lot of emotion and vivid testimony. Rest assured that the Judges can understand this type of behaviour when one gets aroused. However, one should always try and remain calm. And what we gave you instructions to try and stay calm, you did your best to do that. Having said that, I wish you bon voyage back home and every success in that noble profession of yours as a fireman in future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say one word? I would just like to greet all those present. I should like to thank the Court for -- because I had to wait such a long time and on behalf of the fallen fighters and everybody else, thank you for inviting me to come. I can never repay you enough. So thank you, Your Honours. That is all I have left in life. I don't need anything else. I'm not afraid for my own skin. My skin -- I lost my skin and life a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, we have a witness waiting, and it is Mr. -- who?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness Nermin Malovic, Your Honours, and my colleague Ms. Gillett will be conducting the examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber will retire for -- we don't need to retire because our colleague has joined us, which was the reason we were going to retire. But since we're all here, let's have the next witness brought in. As far as the next witness is concerned, the Prosecution will have one hour, and the Defence will have one hour, which means 60 minutes divided by 6 is 10 minutes apiece per Defence team. I would like to take advantage of this time to read an oral decision having to do with a motion submitted by -- let's move into private session first for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's too late. The witness is already in the courtroom so let's move back into open session and I'll deliver the ruling in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Sir, let me check and see if you can understand what I'm saying in your own language. If so, tell me that you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have your first and last name, and date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Nermin Malovic. Date of birth the 14th of February, 1969.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your current occupation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a photographer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir have you ever testified before an international or national court of law about the incidents that took place in 1990s in your country or is this the first time you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is the first time that I'm testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would you now go ahead and read the solemn declaration, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some information to start off with from me. You're going to start off by answering questions put to you by the Prosecutor, Ms. Gillett, whom I'm sure you've already met. Then the Defence will have one hour for the cross-examination, and it will either be the Defence counsel or the accused themselves who will be asking you questions, and a member of the Bench might ask you a question if they deem necessary. I'd like to say good afternoon to Ms. Gillett, and I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good afternoon to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, before the outbreak of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina where were you living?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I was living in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And from when had you been living in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Mostar, as I said, in 1969. I completed elementary school in a place called Jablanica, because my parents lived in Jablanica at the time. I completed first year of secondary school in Jablanica and then continued my secondary school education in Mostar. After that, when I went to Sarajevo to university in 1990, I transferred to Jablanica, and from that time I am an inhabitant of Bosnia-Herzegovina living in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, back in 1991, at that time, were you studying or did you have a job?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was studying, but I also worked as a photographer, freelance, for a number of newspapers and magazines throughout the whole of the -- throughout the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you recall when the outbreak of war took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, although it went little by -- it progressed little by little. First of all there was tension. There were tense situations, and this escalated into all-out conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what about in Jablanica where you say you were living? What was the situation in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: The situation up until the outbreak of the conflict between the BH army and HVO was fairly calm. That is say there weren't any open conflicts. The front line facing the former JNA was about 20 kilometres away from Jablanica as the crow flies, so that there were no direct war operations in the surrounding parts of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You mention the situation was calm up until the outbreak of the conflict between the BH army and the HVO. When was the outbreak of that conflict that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: The beginning of 1992. But I have to say here that at that time in Jablanica where I was there was parallel military authority. There was the BH army command and there was the Croatian Defence Council command, and you had the military police of the BH army and the military police of the Croatian Defence Council as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, as far as your position was concern, did you have any involvement with the army in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I volunteered to join the units of the BH army, offering my services as a photographer, because as I said earlier, I had worked as a freelance photographer for some newspapers and magazines in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. They accepted me, and I started working for the press service of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recall the date on which you started working for the press service?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall the date, but I know it was before the official mobilisation call-up came, a month or two before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What was that date of the official mobilisation call-up?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember the date, but it was early in the summer. It was it hot.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you were with the BH army. Which section of the BH army did you join?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I joined the press service of the BH army, and I took up my duties as a photographer, nothing more. Later, in the course of further organisation within the BH army, the 44th Brigade was formed at Jablanica, the 44th Mountain Brigade, and I started working for the press service of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you recall who the commander of this 44th Brigade was?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: The commander was Enes Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, as far as your work as photographer was concerned, what was the exact nature? What were you expected to do in the role of photographer?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I first have to say that I brought my own equipment to the unit because they had none, and using my equipment I photographed major events of the time, and I have to stress it was not allowed for me to follow BH army units into combat activities because I was at risk of being captured by the enemy, and in that case they would also capture all the material that I had filmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What did you wear in your role within the BH army? Did you wear a uniform or were you in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: At the outset I wore civilian clothing until I received a uniform from friends, because at that time the BH army did not have enough uniforms for such positions as mine. The priority in distributing uniforms was to give them to soldiers on the front line. But later I had a uniform with BH army insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were you also given a rank?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I was always on record as a photographer of the press service.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what about any weapons? Did you carry a weapon?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never received a weapon for the same reason that I described when I was talking about uniforms. The priority was to give weapons to troops on the front line, not those in the rear.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you ever work, was it confined only to Jablanica or did it take you beyond Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part in Jablanica. Occasionally I would go to Mostar and to Konjic, which are neighbouring towns, but never too far. I went to Sarajevo on one occasion. But my job was based and conducted in the area of Jablanica. Municipality, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Moving on into 1993, what was the situation in Jablanica in 1993?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Early in the year, so that would be winter 1993, the situation was as follows: There were two parallel armies, the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council, and parallel officers corps. The armies were distinguishable by uniforms and insignia. Their commands or staffs were in different locations, and their military police forces too. So they were not in the same room or the same building. The situation varied from day-to-day. Sometimes it was tense, depending on the reports we were receiving on the radio and television, and it also depended on the rumours that circulated at the time in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, as far as your work was concerned as photographer, during 1993, what photographs do you recall taking?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I recorded everything that could be noteworthy. Sometimes noteworthy from my point of view, not only what I was ordered to record down the chain of command. Thus I remember that towards the end of 1992, on one occasion I followed members the BH army who were going to take positions on a mountain close to Sarajevo, but I was not allowed to go directly to the front line. I just had the chance to film what was going on in the rear. In 1993, since there were no direct combat activities before the spring, there was nothing particularly interesting to photograph in Jablanica, so that I used that opportunity to go to the neighbouring town of Konjic. That was under the -- under the Serb shelling, and I made some photographs there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: If I can just pick up on a point you made about Jablanica. You said there was nothing interesting prior to the spring of 1993. What happened after that spring of 1993 in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the Croatian Defence Council, who were based in Jablanica at the time, I think it was over the weekend that they left Jablanica. The tentative information that was circulating then was to the effect that they had gone to a military exercise on a plateau called Rizovac, west of Jablanica. Later we found out that the plan of the Defence council was to use this pretext of a military exercise to be able to enter Jablanica in triumph several days later, and I must say most HVO members at the time had left their families behind in their apartments in Jablanica. After the start of that military exercise, Jablanica began to be shelled. The shelling began during the night, and since that was the first real combat activity Jablanica had seen, we were not sure exactly where the shells were falling. We found out later that the shells had not fallen into the centre but a couple of kilometres further out, out of the town of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Your Honour, if I may at this point take the opportunity to make one observation, and this particularly goes to whenever Ms. Gillett brings in a witness. This is all new information that we don't have from the statement. Presumably given the pace of questioning, this information was provided to Ms. Gillett at some point during the proofing session. Now, here we are receiving again all this new information, no proofing notes. We don't have any idea, and yet we're going to be expected 10 minutes each to do cross-examination. This is trial by ambush. This is unfair, and it's done repeatedly when Ms. Gillett specifically does this. And I'm pointing this out because I notice this over and over and over again. So we need explanations. Again I'm going to ask that cross-examination be postponed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Gillett, you have to limit yourself on principle to the witness's written statement, because if you are going to raise issues that are not in the statement the Defence has the right to protest. Now, if you have learned in the meantime that this witness has the knowledge about the shelling of Jablanica, I don't see why that is not in the written statement. He was in the press service of the 44th Mountain Brigade. Ask him what he was doing, what kind of press service it was because this is the first time we're seeing a press officer from the ABH. If I were doing the questioning, I would have approached that question a long time ago, believe me. But please conduct your examination so that it is useful. He may have brought some photos that he had made at the time. They could be of benefit to us perhaps, because he's a photographer after all. That would be perhaps more useful than his impressions about the shelling of Jablanica that other witnesses may later tell us more and better about.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. It is mentioned in the witness's statement as regards the HVO attacking the area of Jablanica back in the early part of 1993, and the witness is, if I can put it this way, putting flesh on the bones of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm entitled to the flesh as well. I cannot cross-examine on the bones. If they're going to bring in flesh, they give it to me in advance. I'm professional. I'm entitled to do my job professionally. I cannot do it. I cannot provide Mr. Prlic with effective assistance of counsel. This is a violation of his rights. And he has human rights as well, not just victims. The accused have human rights and we must respect them they are not being respected by new information leak -- coming out. Now, if she learned of this information, she can pass it on. It's Monday. We should have had it. I presume the gentleman came in on Saturday, they met on Sunday. I don't know but I'm entitled to have this. This happens repeatedly. This is trial by ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we might support that entirely --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We support that entirely, Your Honour. If one looks at what was actually said in the statement that Ms. Gillett has just referred to, it doesn't come within a million miles of indicating that this witness is going to give any evidence at all about that, as indeed there was absolutely zero indication in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, I would like to think that in the same way as I have to deal with matters off-the-cuff that I learn for the first time when I'm on my feet that counsel for the Defence are equally able to deal with the matters that the witness mentions for the first time in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is ridiculous. I don't need a lecture on trial advocacy. There's a huge difference between direct examination and cross-examination. In order to do an effective cross, I need to have the information in advance. I need to check it out. I need to check other documents. This is not just off-the-cuff. I don't need a lecture from someone -- from the Prosecution side on how to prepare my case and how to protect my client. And I think others may want to join in on this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I can move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett, I will give you the floor, but you know that on the basis of a written statement you make a 65 ter summary. You know that this is a gigantic affair. There are 400 of witnesses, millions of documents, and millions of pages. So the Defence counsel, who certainly have less resources than you do in their work, what do they do when a witness appears? They look at the summary and they prepare accordingly. As required, they will also look at the written statement. But Defence counsel will primarily focus on the summary. If the summary makes no reference to the shelling of Jablanica, that is in his written statement in just a tiny little statement, the Defence will necessarily think that you will ask him about Gabela, Heliodrom, detention centres, and the photographs he took, and they are going to prepare for that. That is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, let it be quite clear that the Defence team of General Praljak subscribes to every word my esteemed colleague has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that this Prosecution covers a number of detention centres and municipalities, and you try to sweep over it all with every witness. Taking into account all the problems of time, efficiency, rationality, you should focus witness by witness on the crucial aspects. This witness is a photographer, a press officer, and it is through that lens that you should approach the witness. If I were questioning, I would not be asking about Jablanica. I would be asking him about his profession, his method of work, what he saw in his years as freelance reporter. And as for the shelling of Jablanica, I would do it through another witness. So please focus, Ms. Gillett, to those sections of his witness statement that look much more interesting to me. We have already lost a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever have occasion in 1993 to go to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of the summer of 1993 I received information that prisoners had been freed from the prisoner camps. We called them concentration camps at the time. From Dretelj, that is, and Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: If you can pause there. Do you remember the exact date on which you received this information?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: That was the 28th of August, 1993, and I received the information in the morning. And as I worked with foreign journalists from time to time, and at that time in Jablanica there was a female journalist, and she was not a citizen of the former Yugoslavia, I thought it interesting -- that it would be interesting to her, too -- for her, too, to take photographs and make some video footage of prisoners who had been released who had been released from those concentration camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, do you recall through whom you heard the information that there were these prisoners that were being freed from, as you put it, concentration camps? Do you remember who told you that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I received the information in the command of the 44th Brigade, because the press service of the 44th Brigade was there, their office. After I received the information, I went to find the journalist and organise transport for the two of us from Jablanica to Grabovica, which is at a distance of some 10 kilometres to the south.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, do you recall the name of this journalist and for whom she worked?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I think she was a freelancer, which means she didn't work for any agency specifically. I know that her name was Eileen. I don't know the surname. And I also know that the material, the footage she took she sold later on to the various news agencies in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, when you heard this news and you, as you said, went to find this female journalist, where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: You mean when did I go to find her or when did I go with her?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: No. You mentioned earlier, I'm sorry, about trying to organise transport for the two of you from Jablanica to Grabovica. Did you manage to arrange, to organise that transport?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did organise the transport, and in Grabovica -- we were in Grabovica for half an hour or 45 minutes after receiving that information, that is to say information that the prisoners from these camps would be released. Now, as far as I know in Grabovica we spent from 10.00 to 10.30 in the morning, and we arrived at the hydroelectric power plant in Grabovica, that location, and the upper entrance into the power plant, and there we found a number of prisoners who had already been released.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, if I could just pause there. When you arrived at the hydroelectric plant did you notice whether or not there were any other journalists or photographers or press officers at Grabovica power plant?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice anybody there. At that point in time we were alone, just Eileen and myself. She did her part of the job, and I took photographs of what I thought was interesting.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, what exactly did you see when you got to that power plant? Can you describe what the scene was as you arrived with Eileen?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: We found a certain number of prisoners who were released. They were in an extremely bad state, physically exhausted, and they were not in a good mental condition either. It was obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just said that something -- you just said that something -- something that struck me. They were physically exhausted and mentally not good either. What allowed you to think that they were psychologically affected as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when you look into somebody's eyes, Your Honour, you can see whether it is a stable person, whether they act normal or not. It is sometimes very obvious when a person can not control their behaviour, when the look in their eyes is glassy. Some of these things can be seen on film and others can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Following on from His Honour's question, did you talk to any of these people?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I talked to, I don't know how many of those poor people. Their stories were all one like another. They all looked extremely bad. And if I can tell you -- just the gist of what I found out from them is that they had been imprisoned in camps. They were maltreated, and on that day they had been brought by HVO trucks to the HVO positions near Vrdi in Doljani, and told to get off the trucks and walk towards the positions of BH army, and they obeyed, of course. On the other side of the line they were met by UNPROFOR units and helped them to get onto trucks and APCs, UNPROFOR trucks and APCs. And they were taken from there, from the area of Dreznica, to a slightly safer area where I was at the time, which was the hydro power station of Grabovica. Later on the plan was that they would be taken over by BH army units and transported to Jablanica. Those are -- the basic information that I managed to gather.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know who these people were?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, they were people who came from Herzegovina who were incarcerated or imprisoned or captured by the Croatian Defence Council. They were taken to camps in Dretelj and Heliodrom. They spent some time there, and on the basis of some agreements and negotiations, they were finally released. Let me mention that together with these groups of people who were liberated from the camps there were a number of civilians who were not in the camps, and you can also see that on the photographs. There were elderly women there, younger women, and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know how those other people who had not been in the camps came to be there amongst the people who had come from the camps?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they came to be there, but I just heard that the HVO members went around the villages and told people that they had to collect up the bare essentials, and then they were forced to board trucks and they were transported to the locations I mentioned ago -- that I said before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And from whom did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Dreznica. Well, from the people who were there on the spot, the people who had been transported by trucks, those displaced persons and refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You mentioned these people were from Herzegovina. Do you know what ethnicities, what nationals these people were?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were Muslims. And there were even some comments to the effect that "they were doing this to us just because we were Muslims," the people said. And quite that -- that was obvious from the clothes they wore. You could recognise the traditional type of clothing that the Muslim women wore.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier that you took some photographs and also that the lady, Eileen, that you were with also took some footage, I think you called it earlier. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to be shown Exhibit 00977, which is, as you'll see, a video, and I'm just going to show a short segment from the 19 minutes that it totals. The extract lasts for about one minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just for the benefit of the Court, the subtitles are in B/C/S. The language spoken on the video is French, and the Prosecution have prepared in advance an English transcript for the benefit of the interpreters, and so hopefully although it's equipment commentary on the video it will be able to be followed with some ease. If it could be played now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] On the 31st of August these people arrived in Jablanica. A bit earlier, during their release, their Croat captors amused themselves by forcing them to run under rifle fire. Four people got killed on that occasion. Their skinny bodies bear witness to a horrible treatment they underwent and their statements reveal bestialities. Packed in warehouses, starved, unbearably thirsty. In order to survive they had to drink their own urine. "Detention in the Dretelj and Gabela camps confirm again the daily horror that reigns in detention camps in Bosnia. According to testimonies corrected by the UNHCR, they were constantly beaten and burnt with cigarettes. Some of them died immediately. Certain Croatian soldiers amused themselves by opening fire from automatic rifles on warehouses where they were kept. 30 of them got wounded in that way. In addition to physical there was also mental torture. They had to sing the songs that were derogatory for Muslims. The UNHCR employees claim that those people are nowadays desperate and humiliated. In the Dretelj camp, there are allegedly 2 to 2.500 detainees."

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, did you recognise the place shown in the video?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That's the plateau of the hydroelectric power plant at Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Secondly, do you know who was responsible for taking that video, that particular extract that we've just watched?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be 100 per cent certain, but I think it was filmed by my colleague, Eileen, because after the filming of material of this kind Eileen set off for Sarajevo to hand over the film material she had made, to hand it over to some newspaper. She didn't specify which. Since there was just myself and her there at that time at the hydroelectric power plant, and I took only photographs, not video recordings, I assume that it was Eileen who took this video recording.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, having watched the video did you recognise any of the people that were shown in the video?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise them. They were the same people that I photographed that day or that morning. I don't know their names, but I can recognise them, and I can even recognise the positions at which this was filmed, because there are my -- I have my own photographs from -- taken from the same angle, like this video footage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, we also saw on that video footage, and if necessary we can play it again, in the left-hand corner of the video were the initials HTV, and on the right-hand top corner were the initials TV5. Do you know what the initials HTV stand for?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I can assume. TV houses can buy this from agencies, and that was normal under situations like that. So I assume that a television network bought this material from a news agency and then this was taken over by other networks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know specifically what the initials HTV stand for?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: HTV? Yes, Croatian Television.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, the people that were shown in the video and which you've mentioned several times that you took photographs of, before we get to those photographs, do you know what happened to those people from the point where you saw them in Grabovica? What then happened to them?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: After they arrived in Grabovica, a number of those people were transported to Jablanica where they were put up in the premises of -- or, rather, the sports hall at the elementary school and in the cinema hall in Jablanica and in similar facilities, the ones existing on Jablanica -- in Jablanica municipality. Some of them stayed on in Grabovica in the makeshift sheds that were previously used for workers, to house workers who had worked on the construction of the hydroelectric power plant, their lodgings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm mindful of the time, and as I'm about to move to showing the witness some of the photographs, now might be a convenient time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's take a break. The registrar will tell me how much the time Prosecution has left. We reconvene at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Malovic, moving to the photographs that you mention you took, do you recall how many photographs you took on the 28th of August at Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I think there were a total of seven films, of which three in colour and four black and white.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And how many photographs was each film able to hold?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Thirty-six exposures.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, when you went there and you took those photographs, were you taking them on behalf of somebody or was this of your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just clarify. On that day I went to Grabovica twice. The first time earlier in the morning at my own initiative, and I took with me Eileen, the journalist that I mentioned earlier on. We were in the Grabovica area for about two hours. After that I went back to Jablanica and received instructions from the press service that -- from the press service of the BH army that I was to go again and take photographs of the people who had been released from the prisons, although I had already been earlier on that day in the morning. So I went back to the Grabovica area at about 1.00 or half past 1.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, when you returned, did you return alone or did anybody else accompany you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: I returned with the journalist Eileen, and she continued the journey to Sarajevo, and I assume that she reached Sarajevo that same day, because, after returning to Jablanica for the second time, the duty officer in the police station by which I happened to be passing said that he had seen me 15 minutes prior to that on RTL television. So I assume that Eileen reached Sarajevo that day and that she managed to hand over the material when she did so, which was later distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, the photographs that you took, these some seven films that you've mentioned, what did you do with the films?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: The four black and white films I developed myself in my own laboratory, and the three colour films I wasn't able to develop there because I didn't have the necessary equipment, and seven days later I was with another lady journalist, Maggie O'Kane, she worked for The Guardian, and I worked for her as an interpreter and went to Sarajevo so that the photographs we had taken, to try and get them to England. So those three films were developed by a technician I think from Reuters. Anyway, they used their studio at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mention it was in an attempt to try to get these photographs to England. Did you succeed in getting those photographs to England?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not, for technical reasons. Because of the conditions in Sarajevo, we weren't able to do that. I remember it was a Friday, and the photographs were supposed to be scanned and sent by 12.00 to London. However, there was a power cut in Sarajevo that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, sir. I have to intervene because there's something I don't quite understand here. You were explaining to us that the colour photographs were supposed to be sent to London, but you received instructions from the press service of your brigade to go and take the photographs in the first place. So those photographs, in fact, belonged to the BH army, did they not? So did you have instructions to send them to London or was that on an initiative that you took on your own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was my own initiative, because parallel to the fact that I worked -- rather, was engaged by the BH army as a photographer, I also helped foreign journalists who happened to be in that area during that time, and one of those journalists was Ms. O'Kane, she came several days after these people were released from Dretelj, from Gabela and Heliodrom, and the -- her intention was to go to Sarajevo, but she wasn't able to get through. And so she decided to stay on in Jablanica and write -- and make a story about those people who were released. And I worked as her interpreter. I served as her interpreter on that occasion, but if I -- I needed a permit to go to Sarajevo from the BH army. They showed understanding and gave me permission to go to Sarajevo. But there again, that didn't prove to be successful, this attempt to send the photographs. But the important thing is that we developed the films that day with the help of Reuters, in the Reuters studio.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Once you had these photographs, colour photographs, developed and you said you developed the black and white photographs yourself, what did you do with those photographs?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing special. I just left them there as documentation, and part of that documentation was on the premises of the BH army, in the press service there, and the bulk of the documentation stayed with me. So I made copies of what I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when you were developing the black and white photographs yourself, how did you go about developing those photographs?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the usual way. Everything was done by hand. As I said, I didn't have automatic equipment for development, so that I had to do everything by hand manually with the material that I had. The materials I used weren't that good quality, so some of the photographs were of a poorer quality than they would otherwise have been had we had all the necessary material.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you do anything to the photographs as you were developing them?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing except basic developing. You can't do anything else. You can either develop a film successfully or you destroy the photographs in the process.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Luckily we were successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you -- do you recall being interviewed by somebody from the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Two years ago, an investigator, Romeu Ventura, was his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: At that time did you give photographs to that investigator?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, that is to say two years ago, the situation had already changed so that I had already had the films developed, the ones that were developed in August 1993, and I scanned those films to a CD and handed it over to Mr. Romeu [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, did you do that with all of the photographs or only some of the photographs?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't scan all the photographs. We -- well, we selected the photographs that were the best representatives of the situation in the locality at that time. There were also -- had photographs which we didn't scan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say "we," do you mean Mr. Romeu Ventura? Did he select the photographs? Did he make the choice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told Mr. Ventura that I had seven films, and he said that a selection had to be made of photographs as exhibits and evidence, and among other things Mr. Ventura advised me or us what photographs to select. As I say, the photographs which would best represent and portray what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he chose them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We chose them together. I chose some; he chose others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the questions that the Defence was going to ask, so, Mr. Murphy, I don't think there's any need for you to get up on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just going to ask whether the Prosecution has since then taken into its possession the rest of the photographs, because clearly the Defence would have an interest in seeing them, and I think we would be entitled to in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Of course that's right, and had we taken possession of those photographs then we would, of course, have disclosed them in the normal fashion. We have not taken possession of those further photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that's not the point. The point is that a selection made, and once Ms. Gillett learned of that selection or whoever they communicated it to. It was incumbent upon them to get all of it because that's -- that's what the evidence is, is all those photographs, not what this gentleman thinks accurately depicts the situation as he wants it -- as he wants the Trial Chamber to know, because there may be some photographs that may be exculpatory. And so I think that's why we need to have all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I understand that the purpose of going through the selection process with the investigator was exactly to look at the situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett, at times I am taken aback by the way which the OTP works. You should have taken all the photographs, not just a selection, and then we wouldn't have been wasting all this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution seems to be constantly caught between overloading the Chamber with material that could otherwise be considered duplicative or, indeed, irrelevant, and indeed not providing enough, and it seems that whichever we choose is not the correct way. It has to be said that the purpose of going through the photographs that were in the witness's possession with an investigator was indeed to catch anything that may or may not be exculpatory and otherwise to present the Prosecution case and thereby we're entitled to select the evidence that best represents and goes to support the body of our case, taking into consideration anything that may be exculpatory which was done at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Ms. Gillett's is making two completely contradictory points. The point is not whether these photographs would necessarily be given to the Trial Chamber. Clearly that is a decision which the parties would make. But as far as the second point is concerned, clearly the Defence would be entitled to see whatever photographs this witness produced because it may be that some of them would be of evidentiary value to the Defence and it's a simple point and as Your Honour says it should have been done and we ask that it be done now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is right the Prosecution don't have a duty to go and search for that kind of material that's been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not a matter of searching. We've gone down this road again. Far -- I mean, and this is -- clearly what we're seeing here is the adversarial process at work, because on the -- when you have the inquisitorial the Prosecution has an obligation to search for the truth. Here they're searching for evidence to fit their case, predetermined that these for example guilty, so they're only selecting that. Now, we're not asking them to search. They came across it. They selected. They chose. There's a big difference. So they decided not to collect certain evidence. I'm not asking them to go out and look for it, like Diogenes with a lantern, just try to find out some evidence for the Defence. No. But when they have evidence and it comes their way, what I'm asking and what I'm entitled to is to have all that evidence. So there's a big distinction, and I'm not saying that there may be something in the photographs that might be helpful to the Defence. We don't know. And I think it's erroneous and it's false for Ms. Gillett to say that we don't have a duty to -- to search for, because here they're not searching. The evidence came to them and they had an obligation to collect it on turn it over, and then the Defence can decide what if anything to do with that evidence. That's the way the adversarial process works and that's how this process works as well. Not the ICC, where at least the folks finally woke up and said, Hey, we better get that Prosecutor to look for exculpatory evidence with equal zeal. We don't have that process here. But when they come across evidence, they have to collect it. There lies the difference. And here the evidence came on their lap. They should have collected it. That's what we're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is there any impediment to the Defence going to this witness and, for their evidence, looking for exculpatory pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is no impediment, Your Honour. However -- however -- in this instance. However, we have to keep in mind the equality of arms. We don't have that resources, and that's why to say this could go on with every single witness. That's not how the process should work. It shouldn't be: Let the Defence then try to find this witness and try to get from this witness that evidence. The evidence came to them. Let's just suppose for the sake of argument that we're talking not about photographs but of documents, and then they chose to select certain documents that was helpful to the case and not to select other documents that might have been, might have been helpful to the Defence. Now we have to track down this witness. We have to try to get the evidence from this witness. Maybe the evidence isn't available. Maybe it's been destroyed. The whole point is I'm not saying that we're prejudiced, but what I am saying is that is not an excuse, to say we have no obligations to search for. And I would love to hear Mr. Mundis's explanations for this because I know he agrees with me on this. I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I hate to disappoint --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Mundis. I'm going to give you the floor, but let me just say that, Mr. Karnavas, I completely agree with you. However, simply with respect to the Defence, Article 66 says that on demand the Prosecutor must produce for the Defence documents, material, photographic material, and so on. So once you have these photographs, you could have asked yourselves the question, Have I been provided with all the photographs taken by this photographer? And had you done that, you would have said, No. And I'm going to ask the Prosecutor to give me all the photographs. So you have the possibility of asking the Prosecutor to provide you with the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, with all due respect, Your Honour, it's not always clear from reading a summary or from reading -- looking at the exhibit list that we know that, you know, that there's more material out there. I mean, that is -- we could say this with virtually every witness. That's why we like to take them at their bona fides. That's why I would like to think that they would not be doing a selection process but, rather, they would collect all of it. And I fully understand the issue of duplicity of and overburdening the Trial Chamber, but we're not overburdened with having all that information come our way because we think it might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Mundis, and then we'll end the debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. President. Let's me just be very brief and hit on a couple of issues that I think have been raised that I think need to be responded to. First of all, this witness was interviewed in 2004 and that statement was provided to the Defence. The witness in paragraph 20 of his statement makes reference to having a large photo documentation collection in his possession. So that goes to the point raised by Judge Trechsel and by the Presiding Judge in terms of access to this material. But let me specifically respond to the comment by Mr. Karnavas concerning archives and documents taken from archives as a good example, in our respectful submission, of a point to the contrary of the one that Mr. Karnavas was trying to make. Certainly there are archives available to the parties in the former Yugoslavia that have tens of thousands if not hundreds of thousands of pages of material available. There is simply no way for us to seize entire archival collections totaling hundreds of thousands of pages and disclosing all of that material or reviewing all of that material for purposes of something that might be considered by some Defence team or by some accused to be exculpatory. The nature of the process, of the system in which we are functioning in is that it is a party-driven system, and it's party-driven system whereby the parties produce and look for and search for the evidence to support their cases. The issues that have been arisen with respect to this witness and the photographs and the possibility that there might be an exculpatory photograph are all is subjects that can be dealt with, with the witness in cross-examination. He can be asked about other photographs. That is entirely up to the Defence if they wish to pursue that line of questioning with the witness. But as we've indicated, there are indications in the statement taken more than two years ago that the witness had had in his possession photo documentation, and that photo documentation, the Defence could have sought, they could requested, they could have contacted the witness. They could have contacted the Prosecution. For this to now arise at this point in the proceedings we would suggest is not reasons for any grave concern by anyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, to get on to these photographs and the number that were selected, do you recall, Mr. Malovic, how many photographs were selected?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC
utterances.text: A hundred and ten.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, in the interests of saving time and not having the witness go through all 110 of these photographs in open court, but of course I am prepared to do that should the Trial Chamber require it, I have shown the witness all 110 of these photographs in proofing, and I can now ask him whether -- when we went through that exercise today whether or not those photographs were photographs that he took in order to verify the source of these photos, and my intention was simply to show a sample of, I think it's 29 photographs, and there are reasons that it is a slightly odd number as there may be photographs on which it's helpful to the Trial Chamber for the witness to give any further information that he may have. If the Chamber is happy for the Prosecution to proceed in that manner, than that is what I would propose to do at this stage with an abridged bundle but with the objective of tendering the entire 110 documents through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have no objection to that, and I'm sure I speak for my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then ask him some questions about a few of the photographs taken from -- you said 29. I counted 30. I might be mistaken there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: It could also be my maths, Your Honour, but thank you. Perhaps if the witness can be shown on the screen there front of him in order that we can all see Exhibit 04588.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What I propose, Witness, if you can take a look at the photographs that will be appearing in front of you, and if you come to a photograph that you wish to provide further information about, or, indeed, if you note a photograph that does not relate to the 28th of August, 1993, I would ask you to again give information as to what in particular it is about the photograph, when it was taken, or where it was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question straight away, because while Ms. Gillett was talking I was looking at the 30 photographs, and I note the following: There are some photographs which were apparently taken of people who were released, and we see that they're in a poor physical state. We see that they're very thin. And then there are other photographs of people who look quite well nourished, and there are women and children. Now, the first photograph that we see here that there are both categories; that is that there are a group of individuals who seem to have come out of detention and they're looking over the shoulders of the person in the white shirt, but then there's some women and children, and the woman has a scarf on her head. So is this a group photograph, and is the group made up of two parts, one part people who were released from prison and the other group of people who had come from their homes and taken to this place? Am I wrong, or is that the -- what you saw on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. These were at least two groups of persons. We see people who were released here on that day, released from these prisons, and we can also see civilians there who were told on that day or perhaps the day before that they had to leave their homes and that they would be transported to territory under BH army control. Now, what we see here on this photograph up on our screens is the head of the hydroelectric power plant at Grabovica, and it is the guard hut, and at this particular point in time an announcement had been made to the people who had been released and to the people who had been brought there that food would be distributed -- or bread, rather, bread and biscuits would be distributed. And they tried to introduce some law and order there, but I think that on some of the next photographs you can see that that was very difficult to do. But anyway, this particular photograph illustrates just how many people there were at that point in time in that location. Of course, during the day more people were brought in by UNPROFOR and the number increased as the day progressed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
